decision: Built api/owner-bootstrap.js, a one-time POST endpoint that creates the first authority:owner application_authority_grant. Requires production access enabled and a Google ID token issued within the last ~90 seconds (the same isFreshStepUp freshness check used by the existing employee-session step-up), so the resulting Owner grant is bound to whoever is actually making the live request, never to an identity string this agent was merely told. decision: Built the grant/revoke API for the invite workflow: three new POST endpoints (api/authority-invite.js, api/authority-invite-redeem.js, api/authority-revoke.js) and packages/durability/sql/016_authority_invitation.sql (a new authority_invitation table plus an application_authority_grant.revoked_by column). An existing Owner or Admin with a live employee_session creates a bounded, expiring invitation for someone who has never signed in before; only the invitation token's SHA-256 digest is ever stored, the raw token is returned exactly once in the creation response (no email provider wired yet, per the prior 'hold email for now' decision). Creating the invitation does not grant anything by itself -- the invitee redeems the raw token with their own fresh Google identity, at which point the inviter's authority is re-checked as of that later moment (not assumed still valid from invite-creation time) via packages/authority/src/hierarchy.ts's assertGrantIssuable, the same pure-policy module used everywhere else in the hierarchy. Revocation (api/authority-revoke.js) mirrors this via assertGrantRevocable, requires the same fresh-OIDC-plus-employee-session proof as invite creation, and deliberately does not cascade to grants the revoked one delegated onward (parent_grant_id stays provenance-only, the same rule already applied in lib/application-principal-binding.js). The invite-redeem endpoint's final claim is a conditional UPDATE guarded by state='INVITED'; if two redemptions of the same token race, the loser's just-created grant is immediately self-revoked rather than left as a second live grant, a documented residual race window (not fully eliminated, self-healed) judged acceptable for this pilot's actual usage pattern (one Owner/Admin sending one invite to one specific person), the same risk-tolerance precedent already set by owner-bootstrap.js's own pre-check-then-write pattern. Covered by 22 new unit tests across the three endpoints (sw1-authority-invite.test.mjs, sw1-authority-invite-redeem.test.mjs, sw1-authority-revoke.test.mjs), full npm run conformance passing (591/591 node tests, canon check, traceability check, typecheck all green). Migration 016 was dry-run applied to the isolated preview Neon branch (br-purple-grass-aej54d2x, not production) and its CHECK constraints verified directly (a literal ARRAY['authority:admin'] INSERT round-tripped correctly as text[], and an ACCEPTED-without-resulting_grant_id UPDATE was correctly rejected by authority_invitation_check1), then all test rows deleted, leaving the branch clean. Separately resolved an open technical question raised while writing api/authority-invite.js: whether passing a raw variable-length JS array as a tagged-template parameter for a text[] column (not wrapped in literal ARRAY[...] SQL, unlike the single-scalar ARRAY[$1] pattern owner-bootstrap.js used) is safe with the real, HTTP-based @neondatabase/serverless@1.1.0 driver used in actual Vercel production builds -- the local node_modules/@neondatabase/serverless present in this dev environment is a test-only shim wrapping real Postgres via `pg`, not proof of the real package's behavior. Settled by `npm pack`-ing the actual published @neondatabase/serverless@1.1.0 from the npm registry and reading its source directly: its tagged-template parameter pipeline (prepareQuery -> prepareValue/arrayString) is the exact array-to-Postgres-literal serializer ported from node-postgres, invoked for every parameter before the HTTP request is sent -- confirmed at the source level, not merely inferred. A live round-trip against Neon's HTTP API from this sandbox was blocked by network egress policy (destination host not allowlisted); per this environment's own proxy documentation that is a policy boundary to report, not to route around, and the source-level proof is stronger evidence regardless since it shows the exact code path rather than one observed outcome. decision: Built the Admin 'Employees' management screen: a new nav view in the main SPA (public/employees.js, public/index.html/#employees) backed by two new endpoints (api/authority-directory.js, a read-only roster gated to an active Owner/Admin; api/authority-invite-cancel.js, lets the original inviter or an Owner cancel a still-pending invitation) plus a new standalone redemption page (public/redeem-invite.html, modeled directly on public/owner-bootstrap.html) that an invitee opens to accept an invite with their own fresh Google identity. The invitation link carries the raw token only in the URL fragment (never sent to the server, never in access logs), and the page scrubs it from browser history immediately after a successful redemption. Every sensitive action (create invite, revoke grant, cancel invitation) re-triggers an interactive Google sign-in for a genuinely fresh credential at the moment of that specific request, satisfying each endpoint's independent isFreshStepUp check rather than reusing an older credential -- there was previously no step-up UI anywhere in this frontend at all (the employee_session mechanism from PR #93 had no caller), so this is the first working implementation of that flow, not just for this screen. While building this, found and fixed a real defect in api/authority-invite-redeem.js: it was creating new identity bindings with an empty scopes column, which would have silently blocked every invited operator from actually using their granted operator:* actions (lib/application-principal-binding.js's resolveApplicationPrincipal requires the scope present in application_identity_binding.scopes as well as in the grant -- 'binding scopes remain necessary but are no longer sufficient', per its own RC3 test suite). Fixed by setting scopes to the granted actions on a new binding, and unioning them into an existing binding's scopes on reuse (a second invite to an already-bound person). Dry-run verified directly against the preview Neon branch: the union correctly deduplicated an existing scope while adding the new one. The invite/revoke/cancel actions deliberately do not show role options or targets the caller's own authority couldn't actually grant (an Admin never sees the Admin-tier preset; a self-row never shows a Revoke button), though the backend policy check remains the sole source of truth. Covered by 12 new backend unit tests (authority-directory, authority-invite-cancel) plus updated authority-invite-redeem tests for the scopes fix; full npm run conformance green (604/604 node tests). The two new read-roster queries were dry-run verified directly against the preview Neon branch. The frontend was smoke-tested end to end with a headless Chromium against a static file server, with the Google Identity Services SDK and the four backend endpoints it calls mocked to return the exact response shapes the real, unit-tested endpoints produce: verified the gate/panel visibility toggle, the role picker (4 presets for an Owner), the self/grants/invitations rendering, the full invite-creation round trip including the one-time token-reveal link and the roster refreshing afterward, and separately the standalone redeem-invite.html page's accept and no-token-error paths. This also caught and fixed a real CSS bug (the hidden radio inputs in the role picker were unscoped and could have overlapped unrelated page elements) before it shipped. Not yet executed against real production -- no real invite has been sent or accepted through this UI, and this has not yet been merged to main.

decision: Willie Adofo hit PRODUCTION_APPLICATION_ACCESS_SHA_UNAUTHORIZED live on /join, immediately after BLV2-DEC-033 claimed the gate was fixed. Root cause: a real race in the redeploy pattern used throughout this session. The auto-deploy Vercel triggered for commit 8e5c85f (from the BLV2-DEC-033 governance-record PR merge) started building at 1790091354402; PRODUCTION_APPLICATION_ACCESS_AUTHORIZED_SHA was corrected to 8e5c85f ten seconds later at 1790091364242. Vercel bakes environment variables into the Lambda bundle at build time, not read dynamically at request time, so that specific build almost certainly captured the prior (stale) env var value even though its own git commit was already 8e5c85f -- meaning VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA (correct, 8e5c85f) and the baked-in PRODUCTION_APPLICATION_ACCESS_AUTHORIZED_SHA (stale) mismatched, exactly reproducing the failure Willie saw. This was invisible to the verification done for BLV2-DEC-033: GET /api/build-info only reports deployment metadata (which commit Vercel associates with the deployment), not what value actually got compiled into the running function -- it is not a check of the gate itself. Fixed by forcing a brand-new deployment (mcp__Vercel__create_deployment with forceNew=1) well after the env var had stabilized, guaranteeing a clean env snapshot.
